title: Patient Preferences for Cancer Care Within Hub-and-Spoke Networks: A Discrete Choice Experiment.
content: Hub-and-spoke cancer networks are increasingly used to extend specialty expertise to rural populations; however, patient preferences for how surgical and nonsurgical cancer care should be delivered within these networks are poorly defined. We quantified rural patient preferences and identified distinct preference phenotypes to inform network design. A cross-sectional discrete choice experiment was administered to adult patients at a rural primary care clinic affiliated with an academic cancer center (November 2023 to May 2024). Respondents completed 30 forced-choice tasks evaluating trade-offs among travel time, provider specialization, visit type (in-person vs telemedicine), expert case review (direct, tumor board, or quality oversight), and surgical team experience. Effects-coded conditional logit models generated preference weights. Latent class analysis segmented respondents into preference phenotypes. Among 171 respondents (median age 52 years; 43% Black or people of color), surgical team experience (34%) and surgeon specialization (25%) were most important for surgical care. Fifty-three percent of respondents prioritized a specialist surgeon and a high-volume team and were willing to travel; 39% prioritized in-person visits and accepted indirect case review; and 8% prioritized limiting travel. For nonsurgical care, visit type (35%), travel (27%), and provider type (27%) were the most important factors. Four phenotypes emerged: preference for specialist oncologist (29%), direct expert review (28%), in-person visits (28%), and limiting travel (18%). Rural patients exhibit heterogeneous and treatment-specific preference phenotypes within hub-and-spoke cancer networks. Preference elicitation may enable networks to align specialist deployment, telemedicine infrastructure, multidisciplinary case review, and resource allocation with patient priorities.

title: Real-world study finds direct bictegravir switch effective after first-line HIV treatment failure
content:
Treatment failure on a first-line HIV regimen can mark a critical turning point in long-term care, raising questions about drug resistance, adherence, tolerability and the durability of the next treatment strategy. A real-world study has examined whether people living with HIV who experienced failure on their initial therapy could be switched directly to a single-tablet regimen containing bictegravir, emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide, commonly known as BIC/FTC/TAF. The findings contribute to a growing body of evidence suggesting that the integrase-strand-transfer-inhibitor-based combination may restore viral control for many patients without requiring a prolonged or complex transition between treatment regimens.
BIC/FTC/TAF combines three antiretroviral agents with complementary mechanisms of action. Bictegravir blocks HIV integrase, the viral enzyme required to insert HIV DNA into the genetic material of an infected human cell. Emtricitabine inhibits reverse transcriptase, preventing the conversion of viral RNA into DNA, while tenofovir alafenamide delivers the active tenofovir compound more efficiently into immune cells than older formulations. This allows effective intracellular drug levels to be achieved with lower concentrations circulating in the blood, a characteristic associated with reduced effects on the kidneys and bones compared with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in many clinical settings. The regimen is taken once daily and has a high genetic barrier to resistance, meaning that HIV generally requires multiple changes to its genetic code to become fully resistant to bictegravir.
The real-world investigation focused on a clinically important group: patients whose first-line treatment had not achieved or maintained virological suppression. In routine practice, treatment failure may result from missed doses, drug–drug interactions, gastrointestinal intolerance, inadequate drug exposure, pre-existing resistance or the emergence of resistance during therapy. Distinguishing among these causes is essential, because switching treatment without addressing the underlying problem can lead to repeated failure. A direct move to BIC/FTC/TAF offers a relatively simple strategy, but its success depends on whether the new combination retains activity against the patient’s virus and whether adherence improves or remains consistent after the switch.
According to the study, the switch was associated with renewed control of HIV replication in the real-world population examined. The principal outcome was virological response, generally assessed through plasma HIV-1 RNA measurements after the treatment change. Patients who achieved an undetectable viral load after switching demonstrated that a regimen based on bictegravir could remain effective even when the preceding first-line strategy had failed. This observation is important because clinical trial populations often exclude individuals with complicated treatment histories, inconsistent adherence or uncertain resistance patterns. Real-world cohorts, by contrast, include the clinical variability that physicians encounter in everyday care, providing evidence about how a regimen performs beyond tightly controlled trial conditions.
The results also reinforce the role of treatment simplification in HIV management. A once-daily single-tablet regimen may reduce pill burden and eliminate the logistical complexity associated with multi-tablet combinations. Simplification alone does not guarantee adherence, but it can remove practical barriers, particularly for people managing work, unstable housing, mental-health challenges or other chronic conditions. The direct-switch approach may also reduce the time spent on overlapping or temporary regimens while clinicians await additional laboratory information. For patients and providers, a rapid transition to a potent, well-tolerated combination can be valuable when ongoing viraemia creates a risk of immune deterioration and further resistance development.
Safety and tolerability were another important component of the study. BIC/FTC/TAF is generally regarded as a well-tolerated regimen, although its use still requires clinical monitoring. Bictegravir can produce a modest increase in serum creatinine by inhibiting tubular secretion of creatinine without necessarily causing a genuine reduction in glomerular filtration. Clinicians must therefore interpret kidney-function changes carefully and distinguish this pharmacological effect from true renal injury. Tenofovir alafenamide has a more favourable renal and bone safety profile than tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, but it is not free of risk, particularly in people with pre-existing kidney disease or exposure to other nephrotoxic medicines. Weight changes and metabolic effects, which have been observed with some integrase-inhibitor-based therapies, also remain relevant during long-term follow-up.
The study’s implications extend beyond viral-load measurements. Successful suppression protects the immune system, lowers the risk of HIV-related illness and prevents sexual transmission of the virus when an undetectable viral load is maintained. The principle commonly summarized as “undetectable equals untransmittable” depends on sustained suppression, making continued monitoring essential after any treatment switch. A regimen that restores viral control following first-line failure may therefore produce benefits for both individual health and public health. However, virological response should be interpreted alongside CD4-cell recovery, medication persistence, adverse events, coexisting infections and the patient’s ability to obtain and consistently take the medication.
The findings do not mean that every person with first-line failure should automatically receive BIC/FTC/TAF. Resistance testing, treatment history and adherence assessment remain central to selecting an effective regimen. Integrase resistance is uncommon in many first-line treatment settings but can emerge when an integrase inhibitor is taken inconsistently, and cross-resistance within the drug class may limit future options. Emtricitabine and tenofovir are also affected by certain mutations in the reverse-transcriptase gene. In addition, tenofovir-containing regimens require attention to hepatitis B virus infection, because stopping active hepatitis B therapy abruptly can trigger a potentially serious hepatic flare. Drug interactions must also be reviewed, including those involving polyvalent cations, rifamycin antibiotics and certain anticonvulsants.
As an observational study, the research reflects treatment decisions made in ordinary clinical care rather than a randomized comparison with another regimen. This design allows investigators to capture a broader patient population, but it can also introduce confounding. Patients selected for a direct switch may differ from those given alternative therapies in ways that influence their outcomes, including baseline viral load, resistance history, adherence support or access to healthcare. Follow-up duration and completeness are equally important, because early suppression may not translate into long-term durability. Even with these limitations, evidence from real-world cohorts can help bridge the gap between efficacy demonstrated in clinical trials and effectiveness achieved in diverse healthcare settings.
The study adds support to a treatment strategy that combines potency, convenience and a high barrier to resistance for people confronting first-line HIV treatment failure. Its message is not that a single tablet can replace individualized clinical assessment, but that a carefully selected direct switch to BIC/FTC/TAF may re-establish viral suppression without an unnecessarily complicated treatment sequence. The continuing challenge is to identify why the initial regimen failed, confirm that the new drugs are active, address barriers to adherence and monitor the patient over time. In an era when HIV can be managed as a chronic condition, maintaining durable suppression remains the central measure of success—and real-world evidence will continue to determine how confidently clinicians can apply modern regimens to the full diversity of people living with the virus.

title: «تحت سماء واحدة»... فسحة لفناني الجنوب اللبناني في بيروت
content:
في الطابق السادس من مبنى في منطقة الصيفي، وجدت أعمال 17 فناناً لبنانياً أتوا من الجنوب والبقاع وبيروت سقفاً يجمعها. تختلف الأساليب والمواد والتجارب، فيما يحمل اللقاء أهمية خاصة لفنانين من الجنوب تعطَّل عمل بعضهم بعدما طالت الحرب محترفاتهم وأفقدتهم أماكن اعتادوا الإنتاج فيها.
المعرض هو الجماعي الثاني لـ«مؤسّسة دار زفتا»، وتُنظّمه «زفتا آرت هاوس» في مساحة «نو شيف إنْ ذا كيتشن» في بيروت، بإشراف القيّم الفنّي مُوي عون، ويستمر حتى 30 أغسطس (آب) الحالي. يتنقّل بين الرسم والكولاج والحَفْر الطباعي والتصميم، وتمنح اختلافات اللون والمادة والأسلوب كلّ تجربة صوتها الخاص، من دون أن تفرض الفكرة الجامعة اتجاهاً فنّياً واحداً على المُشاركين.
سبق المعرض أسبوعان من العمل المُشترك، وهي مدّة تضع فكرة «تحت سماء واحدة» في مكان أبعد من عنوان اختِير لحدث فنّي. فالاجتماع حصل قبل العرض، وشارك الفنانون في صنعه قبل لقاء الجمهور بأعمالهم. تتعامل «دار زفتا» مع الجَمْعة على أنها جزء من التجربة وتترك لكلّ فنان مساحته داخل مشروع جماعي لا يشترط التشابُه.
تكتسب هذه الفكرة ثقلاً مختلفاً لدى القادمين من الجنوب. فالحرب التي هشَّمت القرى والأبنية، وصل أثرها إلى المسار الذي تتشكّل من خلاله الممارسة الفنّية. محتَرفات أُقفلت أو تضرَّرت، وأدوات تناثرت تحت الأنقاض، وأعمال اعتادت شروطاً ومكاناً محدَّدَيْن باتت صعبة أو مستحيلة. لذلك يكتسب جَمْع الفنانين لأسبوعين معنى يتّصل أيضاً باستعادة شيء من انتظام العمل الفنّي بعيداً عن تحويل تجربتهم إلى حكاية حرب أخرى.
وتحمل المبادرة لدى صاحب «دار زفتا»، بهجت درويش، امتداداً يرتبط بمستقبل الحركة الفنّية في الجنوب. فوجود هؤلاء الفنانين في بيروت اليوم لا يعني اقتلاع تجاربهم من الأماكن التي نشأت فيها. المعرض محطّة تتيح لهذه الأعمال الوصول إلى الناس، في انتظار اليوم الذي تصبح فيه العودة بها إلى قراها ومدنها ممكنة، ويستعيد الجنوب جزءاً من نشاطه الفنّي والثقافي.
تظهر في بعض اللوحات عمارة تتفكّك إلى مساحات لونية وخطوط، وفي أخرى تتراكم الأشكال حتى يصعب فصل الواحد منها عن الآخر. ثمة ألوان حارَّة ومشبَّعة، ومساحات أكثر خفوتاً، وأعمال تذهب بعيداً في التجريد. وفي إحداها، تمتدّ مساحة رمادية زرقاء تقطعها خطوط كثيرة، في مشهد يترك للسماء حضوراً مُقلِقاً بعيداً عن صفائها المتوقَّع.
ويحمل عمل ميرنا مشنتف فكرة الاجتماع إلى تجربة ذات بُعد بيئي وإنساني. تعاونت الفنانة مع برنامج «نِكْست ستيب» التابع لـ«الجامعة الأميركية في بيروت»، الذي يعمل مع شبان من ذوي الحاجات الخاصة. وجَمَعَ المشاركون علباً معدنية وأغراضاً من منازلهم عوض التخلُّص منها، ثم أعادوا استخدامها مع مشنتف في إنجاز شجرة تشكّلت من جهود نبيلة. وشاركت تاج، ابنة بهجت درويش، مع زملائها ضمن البرنامج في صنع العمل.
تمنح مشاركة تاج هذا الجزء من المعرض دلالة شخصية أيضاً. فالمبادرة التي بدأها والدها بفتح المجال أمام فنانين فَقَدَ بعضهم أماكن عمله، امتدَّت إلى ابنته من جهة مختلفة تماماً. حضرت تاج مع زملائها لتترك بصمتها في المعرض، وتجمع مشاركتها على نحو لافت بين مبادرة الأب وتجربة الابنة، وقد جاء كلّ منهما إلى الفنّ من موقع مختلف.
أرادت مشنتف نقل مفهوم الدمج من مجرّد المشاركة إلى القدرة على التأثير. فهؤلاء الشباب ليسوا متلقّين لنشاط أُعدَّ من أجلهم، ولهم موقع في قضية عامة تعني مستقبلهم مثلما تعني سواهم. يصبح العمل المُشتَرك اعترافاً بمكانهم في المجتمع وبما يستطيعون تقديمه إليه، بعيداً عن النظرة التي تختصرهم في حاجتهم إلى الرعاية أو المساندة. وفي اختيار البيئة، يخرج دورهم من حدود النشاط الفنّي إلى مسؤولية مشتركة يصبحون فيها جزءاً من التعامل مع المشكلة وصنع أثر تجاهها. بذلك يلتقي عمل ميرنا مشنتف مع روح المعرض الذي يجمع أشخاصاً وتجارب مختلفة من دون إلغاء خصوصية أيٍّ منها.
يبقى الفنّ قادراً على وَصْل الناس وحماية الرابط بينهم حين تتبدّل الأمكنة وتضيق الخيارات. تُغادر الأعمال هذا السقف بعد انتهاء المعرض، لكن ما جمعها لا ينتهي بانتهاء موعده. فالفنّ الذي واصل طريقه في وجه الحرب وأتاح لتاج وزملائها مجالاً للمشاركة، يحمل معه إمكان البدء مجدّداً مهما تعثَّرت الظروف. وتحت سماء واحدة، يظلّ للإنسان باب يفتحه حين يظنّ أنّ الأبواب أُغلقت.

title: Una terapia génica ya puede cambiar la vida de niños con una rara epilepsia: "Hasta hace poco, no teníamos herramientas"
content:
Una terapia génica ya puede cambiar la vida de niños con una rara epilepsia: "Hasta hace poco, no teníamos herramientas"
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
De nombre Elsunersen, este fármaco ya se ha probado con éxito en España en una niña con síndrome SCN2A, una mutación que provoca graves crisis epilépticas y un grave retraso en el desarrollo.
Hace unos meses, el Hospital Blua Sanitas Valdebebas fue pionero en España en aplicando un tratamiento para la mutación del gen SCN2A, un síndrome ultrarraro que provoca graves crisis epilépticas de difícil control y, a la larga, retraso en el desarrollo neurológico y muscular, autismo y, consecuencia de ello, una gran discapacidad. “Son niños que suelen tener dificultad de movilidad y necesitan silla de ruedas, que no se comunican y que tienen una vida muy dependiente. Cuando son adolescentes o adultos, además, siguen viviendo con crisis epilépticas en la mayoría de los casos”, explica Ángel Aledo, codirector del Centro Integral de Neurociencias de Valdebebas.
Gracias a este tratamiento, que fue aplicado con éxito en una niña diagnosticada nada más nacer, el futuro de los niños puede cambiar, pues, aunque aún hay que ver cómo se desarrolla a lo largo de los años, de momento, ya han conseguido frenar las crisis epilépticas, causantes de los problemas en el desarrollo, en un 90%.
El tratamiento, llamado Elsunersen está en fase experimental, pero, por lo que se está observando en la primera niña tratada en España, los resultados son más que prometedores.
Qué es Elsunersen y cómo funciona
Elsunersen es una terapia génica de precisión basada en un oligonucleótido antisentido, un fragmento genético diseñado para reducir la expresión del gen SCN2A cuando existe una mutación que hace que funcione en exceso. Se administra cada cuatro semanas mediante una punción lumbar para llegar al líquido cefalorraquídeo y actúa sobre el cerebro. “De esta forma se intenta reducir la hiperexcitabilidad de las neuronas que está detrás de las crisis epilépticas y del problema de neurodesarrollo. En este caso, por tanto, podemos actuar sobre el mecanismo que origina la enfermedad y no únicamente sobre sus síntomas”, explica Ángel Aledo.
En este caso, el tratamiento empezó el 20 de febrero de 2026, cuando la niña tenía apenas unas semanas de vida. “Las crisis epilépticas, que eran diarias, cedieron cinco días después de esa primera administración. La precocidad es especialmente relevante porque se trata de uno de los casos tratados a menor edad descritos hasta ahora a nivel internacional”.
Las crisis epilépticas, que eran diarias, cedieron cinco días después de esa primera administración
La importancia del diagnóstico precoz
Habitualmente, sin tratamiento, los niños con esta mutación desarrollan una “encefalopatía epiléptica del desarrollo”, en la que problema genético y las crisis epilépticas repetidas en momentos vulnerables del desarrollo de un cerebro impiden que el bebé adquiera hitos del neurodesarrollo como seguir la mirada, sonreír o sostener el cuello. Por este motivo, cuanto antes se empiece con el tratamiento, mejor como ha sido este caso, pues los niños con esta mutación, debido a las crisis epilépticas, van acumulando daño y discapacidad con el paso del tiempo.
“El diagnóstico genético permitió utilizar primero los medicamentos antiepilépticos convencionales más eficaces y tener una pequeña mejoría, pero aun así las crisis epilépticas seguían hasta iniciar Elsunersen”, narra Aledo. “En estas epilepsias, llegar pronto al diagnóstico es especialmente importante porque permite elegir el tratamiento en función del mecanismo de la enfermedad y actuar durante una etapa crítica del desarrollo cerebral. En una enfermedad que afecta al cerebro desde los primeros días de vida, controlar antes las crisis puede limitar el tiempo durante el que esa actividad epiléptica y el defecto genético subyacente interfiere con el neurodesarrollo”.
Aun así, aunque el fármaco aún está en investigación, los datos que se conocen hasta el momento hacen pensar que también podría producir ser eficaz aplicado más tarde. “En el ensayo EMBRAVE, realizado en pacientes de entre 2 y 12 años, se observó una reducción significativa de las crisis y el beneficio se mantuvo durante el seguimiento”.
Prudencia y esperanza
Desde el Hospital Blua Sanitas Valdebebas están muy esperanzados, pues tras cuatro dosis las crisis habían prácticamente desaparecido y los electroencefalogramas mostraban una reducción del 90% de la actividad epiléptica. Además, había mejorado el tono muscular, comenzaba a fijar la mirada y a controlar los músculos del cuello y había podido pasar de la alimentación por sonda a comer por vía oral. “Son cambios clínicamente muy relevantes, aunque el seguimiento sigue siendo todavía corto y debemos interpretarlos con prudencia”, aseguran.
Y es que, aunque las perspectivas son muy buenas, la paciente, que aún es un bebé, va a necesitar un seguimiento neurológico estrecho y continuado, por lo que los médicos tienen esperanzas, pero son prudentes. “El objetivo no consiste únicamente en mantener controladas las crisis epilépticas, sino en acompañar su desarrollo y comprobar cómo evoluciona con el paso del tiempo. La paciente ya sigue fisioterapia, logopedia y estimulación temprana y se está optimizando la medicación antiepiléptica”, insisten.
“Que las crisis hayan prácticamente desaparecido y que estén apareciendo avances motores, visuales y en la alimentación son señales muy positivas, sobre todo teniendo en cuenta la gravedad inicial. No obstante, todavía no podemos saber cuál será su desarrollo a largo plazo ni afirmar que vaya a ser completamente normal, porque las crisis comenzaron a los pocos minutos de vida y el cerebro ya estuvo expuesto al mal funcionamiento del gen y a una actividad epiléptica muy intensa. Ahora tenemos que observar su evolución durante años y ayudarla a alcanzar el máximo desarrollo posible”.

Un futuro esperanzador para miles de niños en todo el mundo
Terapias como esta pueden cambiar radicalmente la vida de una persona, pueden suponer vivir una vida plena o marcada por la discapacidad, e incluso en muchos otros casos, la diferencia entre una vida larga y una muerte prematura. Por eso, desde la neurología en general están esperanzados, pues terapias como esta demuestran que estamos entrando en una etapa muy diferente de esta especialidad. “Hasta hace pocos años, ante muchas enfermedades genéticas podíamos tratar las crisis epilépticas u otros síntomas, pero no teníamos herramientas para actuar específicamente sobre el mecanismo molecular que los provocaba. Terapias como esta permiten empezar a hacerlo en determinadas enfermedades y abren la puerta a tratamientos mucho más personalizados”.
Si la ciencia avanza en este sentido, desde Sanitas no dudan en que veremos cada vez más tratamientos dirigidos a alteraciones genéticas concretas, “especialmente a medida que mejore la capacidad para diagnosticar estas enfermedades de forma precoz. Para nosotros, este caso demuestra el valor de conectar diagnóstico genético, neurociencias clínicas, y acceso a terapias avanzadas dentro de un mismo modelo asistencial”.
Aun así, insisten en que no se debe generalizar, ya que muchas de estas terapias siguen en investigación, se necesitan más pacientes y más años de seguimiento para conocer su efecto real sobre el neurodesarrollo y la calidad de vida. El objetivo, es por tanto, “seguir avanzando en medicina de precisión y participar en el desarrollo de nuevas opciones para enfermedades neurológicas que hasta ahora tenían alternativas terapéuticas muy limitadas”.

title: Lagos to host 15,000 athletes for national intermediate games
content:
Lagos is set to host about 15,000 young athletes aged between 15 and 18 for the maiden National Intermediate Games scheduled to hold from October 1 to 15, 2026.
The athletes are expected to compete in 23 compulsory and five optional sporting disciplines across 10 venues in the state.
In a post obtained from the state’s X handle on Thursday, the Chairman of the Local Organising Committee, Sam Egube, disclosed this during a media parley in Lagos, describing the games as a major platform for youth development, talent discovery and national unity.
Egube said the competition would provide opportunities to identify and nurture young athletes with the potential to advance to the National Sports Festival, continental competitions and eventually the global sporting stage.
He said, “The games will provide a strategic pathway for grassroots sports development and help us identify and nurture the next generation of Nigerian sporting talents.”
According to him, Lagos would leverage its experience in hosting major international sporting events to deliver a world-class competition.
“Lagos has built considerable experience in hosting major sporting events, and we are bringing that experience to bear to ensure a successful maiden edition,” he said.
Egube added that the games would also contribute to the local economy by creating opportunities for small businesses while allowing visitors to experience the state’s culture, hospitality and tourist attractions.
Commissioner for Youth and Social Development, Mobolaji Ogunlende, said preparations for the event were progressing rapidly, noting that the state had only 37 days to the commencement of the games at the time of the media parley.
He assured athletes, officials and visitors of a safe and memorable experience.
Ogunlende also appealed to the media to provide accurate information about the event, promote Lagos’ attractions and reassure participants of the state’s readiness to host the games.
Commissioner for Information and Strategy, Gbenga Omotoso, said the state was determined to deliver an excellent first edition.
Omotoso said the initiative was designed to bridge the gap between young sporting talents and professional athletes.
“The idea is to identify these young talents early, develop them and provide them with the opportunity to become future stars,” he said.
He disclosed that various subcommittees had been established to coordinate critical areas of the games, including security, transportation and athletes’ welfare.
Omotoso added that Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu had personally inspected some of the sporting facilities as part of preparations for the competition.
The Director-General of the Lagos State Sports Commission, Lanre Fatodu, described Lagos as a “serial trailblazer” and expressed confidence in the state’s ability to deliver a successful competition.
“Lagos is a serial trailblazer, and we will draw on our wealth of experience in hosting major sporting events to deliver a successful National Intermediate Games,” Fatodu said.
The organisers said the games would go beyond sporting competition, serving as a platform for talent discovery, youth empowerment, national unity and grassroots sports development.
With 15,000 young athletes expected to converge on Lagos, the inaugural National Intermediate Games is expected to provide a significant platform for discovering and developing Nigeria’s next generation of sporting stars.

title: Africa’s tech leapfrog: From mobile to banking to AI revolution
content:
South Africa leapfrogged landlines in the 1990s, moving straight to mobile networks.
Africa’s developers are entering a new phase of technological leapfrogging, with artificial intelligence set to drive growth and innovation across the continent.
Speaking at the Amazon Web Services (AWS) Sub‑Saharan Africa Summit at Gallagher Estate in Midrand on Wednesday, General Manager Jyoti Ball said Africa’s ability to skip traditional stages of development has given it a unique advantage.
Mobile revolution
“Has there ever been a more exciting time to be a developer? We are living at the epicentre of multiple, simultaneous golden ages – space travel, AI, robotics – each reinforcing the other,” Ball told delegates, echoing Jeff Bezos’s description of the current era as one defined by overlapping breakthroughs.
She pointed to the continent’s mobile revolution as a clear example of leapfrogging.
“In the early 1990s, South Africa had only four million mobile connections for a population of 40 million. Instead of waiting for landlines to expand, the country moved directly into mobile networks. Today, there are more than 115 million mobile connections for 65 million people – nearly two per person.”
Banking infrastructure
Ball added that Africa also bypassed traditional banking infrastructure, building mobile payment systems that now lead the world.
“The continent has more mobile money accounts than any other region, with one in five Africans relying on mobile money as their only financial account. In 2023 alone, mobile money platforms processed 92 billion transactions worth $1.4 trillion.”
Leapfrogging AI
She argued that the same leapfrogging is now happening with AI.
“Africa didn’t wait for landlines or bank branches. And now, it isn’t waiting to build AI the old way. Developers are already using language models in African languages, computer vision to detect crop diseases, and generative tools to build products faster than ever before.”
Examples include Jubilee Insurance, which built an AI‑powered claims agent in just 20 days, and startups applying AI to monitor millions of trees across multiple countries.
AI market
Ball noted that the AI market in Africa is projected to reach $16.5 billion by 2030, growing at 27% annually, with the IMF estimating it could add four percentage points to GDP if the right foundations are laid.
According to AWS, the company has invested $819 million in Africa since 2018, committed a further $1.5 billion, and trained one million people in cloud and AI skills.
“What excites me most is Africans not just consuming AI, but building their own AI. That’s the next leapfrog,” Ball said.
The summit underscored a broader message: Africa’s developers are not simply catching up, but are positioned to lead in shaping AI solutions for local and global challenges.

title: Gwangju Biennale restores ‘Taiwan’ name: report
content:
The Gwangju Biennale Foundation has agreed to allow Taiwan’s exhibitors to use the name “Taiwan” in the exhibition venue and in official documents and promotional materials, South Korea’s Munhwa Broadcasting Corp reported yesterday.
The foundation made the decision after considering Taiwan’s stance that it would withdraw from the exhibition, opening on Sept. 5th, if the name could not be used, the broadcaster said.
Earlier yesterday, the Ministry of Culture urged the foundation to respond by today to its request to restore the name of Taiwan’s participating exhibition from “NTMoFA,” the acronym for the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts, to “Taiwan Pavilion.”
Photo: CNA
In a statement, the ministry “sternly protested” the foundation’s and the Asia Culture Center’s (ACC) refusal to restore the name and what it described as efforts to prevent Taiwan Pavilion personnel from entering the venue to set up the exhibition, originally scheduled to begin on Tuesday last week.
The statement did not specify what action would be taken if the organizers failed to respond.
The ministry said it issued statements on Monday and Wednesday last week explaining that the name “Taiwan Pavilion” was changed to “NTMoFA” without discussion or prior notice.
It also pointed to a statement issued yesterday by the Taiwan Pavilion’s curator and artists, titled “You Must Change Your Name,” which accused the foundation of repeatedly ignoring the museum’s objections to the name change and said an artistic institution should not become a tool for suppressing self-identification.
Over the past week, the ACC has refused to allow Taiwanese exhibitors to enter the venue to set up the exhibition, citing the lack of an official document from the foundation, the ministry said.
Although the museum received a copy of a foundation letter permitting them to enter the venue on Wednesday, the ACC continued to say it had not received the document and refused to allow NTMoFA representatives to enter, the ministry said.
After a museum representative took photographs to document the incident, ACC venue staff demanded to inspect the person’s phone and asked them to delete the photographs, it said.
Furthermore, the foundation proposed relocating Taiwan’s exhibition to an alternative storage space that was much smaller than the original site, the ministry said.
Members of the international artist community and art workers have also spoken out, urging the foundation not to use its authority to determine the name under which participants are identified and to restore the name “Taiwan Pavilion” as soon as possible, it said.
Earlier, the foundation said it would neither intervene in nor censor the content or expression of exhibitions, and would continue negotiations to ensure that the NTMoFA’s exhibition proceeds as planned.
The foundation said the exhibition is purely an artistic partnership and that it has never intervened, nor would intervene, in the NTMoFA pavilion’s curation, selection of works, installation methods or the expressions of its curator and artists.
It said it was concerned that the controversy had developed into a political and diplomatic issue, adding that the dispute stemmed from differing interpretations of administrative procedures and the agreement concerning the pavilion’s participating institution and how it should be labeled in official materials.
The foundation said that the agreement signed on Jan. 12 clearly identified the Gwangju Biennale Foundation and the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts as the parties involved and that its implementation was based on that agreement.
In contrast, the ministry has insisted that the original agreement was that the name “Taiwan Pavilion” would be used and was only changed by the foundation in June.
The foundation argued that the labeling used in official documents and promotional materials should be distinguished from the exhibitor’s own self-identification.
Regarding the difficulties encountered by Taiwan’s exhibitors, the foundation said it had signed a contract with the venue for use of the exhibition space, but the contract did not specify the countries or institutions that would hold exhibitions there.
It said it would ask the ACC to open the space and cooperate with the installation and exhibition operations so that the NTMoFA’s exhibition can proceed as planned.
If further delays or difficulties arise, the NTMoFA could consider using an alternative space inside the biennale venue, it added.
The foundation concluded that both the autonomy of exhibitors and the official operations stipulated in the agreement should be respected, saying the priority was not for the two sides to “more loudly propagate their own stance,” but to quickly find a workable solution that would allow the exhibition to be held as scheduled.
Founded in 1995, the Gwangju Biennale in South Korea is Asia’s oldest and most prestigious biennial of contemporary art.
In an August titled “Who is Afraid of the Name ‘Taiwan Pavilion,” the coalition of South Korean artists has criticized the biennale for disregarding artists’ right to identify their own nationality and failing to engage in discussion and consultation, and said it is deeply troubling that such “political censorship” occurred in Gwangju, a city known as South Korea’s “sacred ground of democracy.”
“The Taiwan Pavilion case reflects a broader problem in the international art world, where discrimination based on nationality, race, gender, religion or political views has led to artworks being altered or removed, exhibitions and public statements being canceled, and artists and cultural workers being silenced,” the group said.

title: Del espacio al quirófano: la prótesis pionera que imita al hueso y abre una nueva vía en la sanidad pública
content:
Del espacio al quirófano: la prótesis pionera que imita al hueso y abre una nueva vía en la sanidad pública
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
La 'pieza' está hecha de un metamaterial empleado también en la industria aerospacial.
Una tecnología empleada en la industria aeroespacial ha llegado al quirófano con un objetivo muy concreto: crear prótesis prácticamente a medida del paciente. El Hospital Gregorio Marañón de Madrid ha diseñado, fabricado e implantado la primera prótesis personalizada de metamaterial del mundo, un dispositivo que reduce drásticamente el peso y el coste frente a las prótesis convencionales y que podría abrir el camino hacia soluciones de medicina hiperpersonalizada dentro de la sanidad pública.
Una de las grandes diferencias está precisamente en el peso. Frente a los varios kilos que pueden alcanzar las prótesis estándar, estos nuevos dispositivos pueden pesar apenas unos cientos de gramos. También cambia el coste: de las decenas de miles de euros de algunas prótesis convencionales a alrededor de 3.000 euros por la impresión 3D de esta pieza, según explicaron durante su presentación Rubén Pérez, cirujano oncológico del Gregorio Marañón y subdirector de su Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria, y Luis Saucedo, ingeniero de la Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (UPM).
Pero la innovación va más allá de hacer una prótesis más ligera. El implante está pensado para imitar al hueso e integrarse con él, en lugar de limitarse a sustituirlo. Su estructura hueca permite rellenarlo con injertos óseos, de forma que el hueso queda entrelazado en el interior de la pieza metálica. Según explicó Pérez, esto permite que “el cuerpo humano lo tome como suyo”, evitando el rechazo mecánico. Al ser más ligero e integrado, el objetivo es también que el paciente pueda recuperar su actividad funcional anterior sin los desequilibrios asociados a prótesis mucho más pesadas.
Barras a escala milimétricas
La tecnología empleada procede del ámbito aeroespacial. Las prótesis de metamaterial están constituidas por barras a escala milimétrica capaces de recrear la forma y la función del hueso. En este caso, el dispositivo consiste en una aleación de titanio fabricada mediante impresión 3D y diseñada de forma “hiperpersonalizada”. “Que se diseñen soluciones a medida en la industria existen, pero que se haga por parte de un hospital es más raro, y siendo un hospital público universitario, más todavía”, destacó Pérez. Para el cirujano, se trata de “una fortaleza de nuestro sistema nacional de salud porque nos permite tener entorno académico y científico al servicio del paciente”.
El primer gran resultado de la colaboración entre los cirujanos del Marañón y los ingenieros de la Politécnica tiene nombre propio. Pierre, un hombre de 38 años con un sarcoma de alto grado en la tibia, se enfrentaba a la amputación como única alternativa. La prótesis personalizada permitió salvarle la pierna y, un año después de la intervención, hace una vida normal y puede caminar sin muletas. Su implante pesa 300 gramos y es capaz de soportar 500 kilos de carga. Su resistencia quedó además puesta a prueba de manera accidental: Pierre sufrió una aparatosa caída que le fracturó huesos de la pierna contraria, mientras que el implante soportó el impacto.

title: Tiene 300 estudiantes: una escuela investiga un valioso suplemento para la producción de una provincia
content:
En un colegio agropecuario de Gobernador Gregores, Santa Cruz, se analiza el impacto del pellet proteico-energético producido con materia prima local para la ganadería ovina
- 6 minutos de lectura'
EL CALAFATE, Santa Cruz.- En la Patagonia, donde las distancias y los costos de producción suelen marcar el destino de muchos proyectos agropecuarios, una experiencia que acaba de comenzar en Gobernador Gregores busca comprobar si es posible generar un alimento ovino eficiente utilizando materias primas producidas en Santa Cruz. La respuesta empezará a surgir en las próximas semanas, a partir de un ensayo que combina innovación, educación y agregado de valor local.
El puntapié inicial lo dio la primera planta peletizadora de Santa Cruz, inaugurada recientemente por el Consejo Agrario Provincial en Gobernador Gregores con el objetivo de transformar materias primas que se producen en la provincia en alimento con valor agregado para mejorar la alimentación animal de la zona.
Con la producción en marcha, la Escuela Agropecuaria Provincial N.º 1 “Heroínas de Malvinas” aportó fardos de alfalfa producidos en la escuela para los pellets, -a los que se le sumaron también granos producidos en Santa Cruz para aportar proteína al alimento-, en tanto que presentaron un ensayo para realizar las pruebas de rendimiento en la escuela y aportar los resultados para ajustar o mejorar la producción del alimento.
Para poner a prueba el rendimiento de los pellets, la escuela conformó dos lotes de 50 ovejas preñadas por inseminación artificial provenientes de la majada general de la escuela. Un lote recibe diariamente medio kilogramo por animal de suplemento proteico-energético elaborado en la planta local, mientras que el otro permanecerá sin suplementación. Ambos grupos continuarán bajo las mismas condiciones de pastoreo y manejo, con acceso permanente al agua, de manera que las diferencias observadas puedan atribuirse al uso del alimento.
“Lo que estamos haciendo es una prueba a campo y real de cuál será el impacto del pellet proteico-energético, principalmente sobre las variables de interés en términos productivos o en términos de la condición del animal”, detalló a LA NACION Germán Seeber, ingeniero agrónomo y director de la escuela que funciona en doble turno.
El ensayo se concentra en el último tercio de gestación, una etapa clave para el desempeño productivo de las madres y el desarrollo de los futuros corderos. Durante al menos 45 días se realizará un seguimiento permanente para evaluar la evolución de los animales.
Los docentes y los estudiantes registran las variables como peso vivo, condición corporal, peso de vellón, peso de los corderos al nacer, porcentaje de parición, porcentaje de señalada y controles fecales, con el fin de comparar la respuesta de ambos grupos y determinar la eficiencia de la suplementación.
Además del interés productivo, la iniciativa tiene un fuerte componente formativo. Los estudiantes participan en cada una de las etapas del trabajo: desde la planificación del ensayo y la formulación de las raciones hasta el registro, sistematización y análisis de la información obtenida. También intervienen en los encierres diarios, la distribución del alimento y el seguimiento de los animales.
Los resultados serán presentados en las próximas “Olimpíadas Nacionales” bajo el nombre de “Suplementación estratégica periparto en ovinos” por los estudiantes de 6 año Selena Rabe, Simón Martínez , Millalonco Aylén, Eric Pérez. Se trata del encuentro educativo y de competencia técnica en la Argentina donde los estudiantes de escuelas agrotécnicas muestran sus conocimientos sobre la producción ovina que este año será en Catamarca.
La investigación que aportará información valiosa para la ganadería ovina de Santa Cruz es llevada adelante desde el sector docente por Mónica Infante, jefa sectorial y coordinadora de Prácticas Profesionalizantes y los auxiliares de la sección Ganadería: Bernardo Jara, Franco Sanz, Adriana Brizic, Agostina Poggio y el profesor Martín Kaschewski.
Desde el Consejo Agrario Provincial destacaron que el proyecto forma parte de una estrategia orientada a fortalecer la producción local y generar nuevas oportunidades para el campo santacruceño. “El gobernador Claudio Vidal nos pidió recuperar la cultura del trabajo y transformar las decisiones de gestión en herramientas concretas. Esta planta es una muestra de ese camino: producir, agregar valor y generar oportunidades para nuestros productores”, señaló el presidente del organismo, Hugo Garay.
La articulación territorial de la experiencia está a cargo del delegado del CAP en Gobernador Gregores, Jorge Poclepovic, mientras que el director de la Escuela Agropecuaria, Germán Seeber, participa del seguimiento de los animales y del desarrollo técnico del ensayo. La Escuela Agropecuaria tiene dos tecnicaturas, una en Producción Agropecuaria y la otra en Mecanización Agropecuaria. “Por la dinámica productiva de la provincia y las condiciones de Patagonia Sur, los dos programas de estudio están enfocados a lo productivo regional, con las particularidades y la orientación de su zona”, detalló Seeber.
“La escuela cuenta con 300 estudiantes, 130 docentes -algunos con poca carga horaria y otro con carga horaria completa-, tenemos un albergue estudiantil donde estudiantes se hospedan acá durante todo el año mientras cursan y el terreno de la escuela son 1200 hectáreas donde tenemos una parte de producción intensiva bajo riego”, explicó el director y aclaró que en la zona la mayoría del riego en las chacras es gravitacional, por manto, por inundación o por surco.
La escuela cuenta con invernaderos y cinco secciones productivas: agricultura, huerta, ganadería, industria y granja, además de un aula móvil y distintos talleres de soldadura, motores, mecanización, carpintería y electrónica entre otros. Funciona todo el día, de 7 de la mañana a 19, con doble turno, y los estudiantes tienen materias de distintos campos de conocimiento. Hacen una parte de las clases en el aula dentro de la escuela en tanto que realizan la parte práctica en el predio.
Más allá de los resultados que arroje la prueba, la experiencia ya permite mostrar una cadena productiva integrada: materias primas producidas en la provincia, procesamiento local mediante la planta peletizadora y validación técnica a través de una institución educativa especializada.
En estos días, granos de avena cosechados este verano en la Estancia Alice, a kilómetros del glaciar Perito Moreno, producidos por la empresa AgroCalafate, partieron a la planta de Gregores ubicada a 500 km de aquí. La cosecha fue parte de un proyecto que involucró a la empresa estatal Santa Cruz Puede, que impulsa, entre otras iniciativas, la producción de alimento para ganado a partir de acompañar diferentes etapas del proceso.
Dentro de poco más de un mes comenzarán a conocerse los primeros datos. Entonces, los registros obtenidos en la escuela determinarán si este alimento santacruceño puede transformarse en una alternativa concreta para mejorar la productividad ovina y aportar una nueva herramienta a los productores de la provincia.

title: Los hidratos de carbono de alta calidad reducen el riesgo de mortalidad, sobre todo por cáncer
content:
Una dieta rica en hidratos de carbono de alta calidad -fibra y cereales integrales- reduce el riesgo de muerte, especialmente por cáncer, en personas con riesgo cardiovascular elevado.
Las personas que consumen hidratos de carbono de más calidad tienen un menor riesgo estadístico de mortalidad, especialmente por cáncer, según concluye un estudio internacional de la Universidad Rovira i Virgili (URV), el Instituto de Investigación Biomédica Cataluńa Sur (IRB-CatSud) y el Centro de Investigación Biomédica en Red de la Fisiopatología de la Obesidad y Nutrición (CIBEROBN).
La investigación, coordinada por Jordi Salas-Salvadó y Héctor Vázquez-Lorente, investigadores del Departamento de Bioquímica y Biotecnologia de la Universidad Rovira i Virgili (URV), destaca la importancia de priorizar alimentos ricos en fibra, como las frutas, las verduras, las legumbres, los frutos secos y los cereales integrales, frente a los productos elaborados con harinas refinadas o las bebidas azucaradas.
"Durante ańos, buena parte del debate sobre los hidratos de carbono se ha centrado en la cantidad que se consume. Pero cada vez hay más evidencias de que la calidad de los alimentos que los aportan puede ser determinante para la salud", seńalan los autores de la investgación que se publica en la revista Food & Function.
El equipo investigador ha trabajado con datos de 7.210 participantes del proyecto Predimen, uno de los ensayos clínicos más importantes sobre dieta mediterránea y salud cardiovascular, detalla la URV en un comunicado. Los participantes —hombres de entre 55 y 80 ańos y mujeres de entre 60 y 80 ańos— presentaban un riesgo cardiovascular elevado y fueron seguidas durante un periodo medio de seis ańos. Durante este tiempo se registraron 425 defunciones, de las cuales 169 fueron por cáncer y 103 por enfermedades cardiovasculares.
Para valorar la calidad de los hidratos de carbono de la dieta y no limitarse a contabilizar los gramos de hidratos consumidos, el equipo investigador utilizó el Carbohydrate Quality Index (CQI), que combina cuatro características de los alimentos ricos en carbohidratos: el contenido en fibra, la proporción de cereales integrales respecto de los refinados, el índice glucémico -la velocidad con la que un alimento hace aumentar la glucosa en sangre- y la proporción de hidratos de carbono procedentes de alimentos sólidos en comparación con las bebidas azucaradas.
Los resultados revelan que las personas que siguieron una peor dieta en cuanto a la calidad de los hidratos que consumían presentaron un 28% más de riesgo de morir por cualquier causa y un 48% más de riesgo de morir por cáncer que aquellas con un consumo de carbohidratos de mejor calidad.
"Tradicionalmente se ha prestado mucha atención a la cantidad de hidratos de carbono de la dieta, pero nuestros resultados indican que su calidad puede ser aún más relevante para preservar la salud y aumentar la esperanza de vida", subrayan en un vídeo Jordi Salas-Salvadó, catedrático distinguido de Nutrición de la URV, investigador ICREA y coautor del estudio junto a Héctor Vázquez-Lorente.
El análisis también ha permitido identificar qué componentes de los hidratos de carbono de calidad tienen más peso en esta asociación. Los beneficios se explican principalmente por un consumo más elevado de fibra y cereales integrales. "Las personas con una ingesta más baja de fibra presentaban un 51% más de riesgo de morir por cualquier causa y un 72% más de riesgo de morir por cáncer. También se observó un aumento del riesgo entre los participantes que consumían menos cereales integrales, mientras que el índice glucémico, analizado de forma aislada, no mostró una relación significativa con la mortalidad.
Según los investigadores, "estos beneficios podrían explicarse porque los alimentos vegetales ricos en fibra también aportan vitaminas, minerales y otros compuestos bioactivos que contribuyen a mejorar la salud metabólica y a reducir el riesgo de enfermedades crónicas. Por ello, concluyen que "una estrategia sencilla para mejorar la salud pasa por priorizar frutas, verduras, legumbres, frutos secos y cereales integrales, y reducir el consumo de bebidas azucaradas y productos elaborados con harinas refinadas".

title: 50 Years of Bronx River Clean-Up Efforts Lead to the First Otter Sighting in a Century
content:
Nature seems to be healing along the Bronx River in New York.
This week, the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) confirmed the recent appearance of an North American river otter in the Bronx section of the river—the first such sighting recorded in about a century. Though it’s not clear whether otters en masse have returned to the area, the discovery is likely another sign that decades-long efforts to clean up the river are indeed going well.
“There are moments in conservation that remind us why this work matters, and this is one of them,” said Craig Piper, director of the Bronx Zoo and interim executive vice president of Zoos & Aquarium at WSC, in a statement released by the organization Tuesday.
A chance sighting
The otter was actually documented earlier this June by scientist R.J. Hawkins, via a motion-activated camera. Hawkins was conducting long-term camera trap monitoring for wildlife along the river overseen by the WCS’s Education Department based at the Bronx Zoo. The WSC manages four accredited zoos and one aquarium in New York City.
“When I first reviewed the images, I could hardly believe what I was seeing,” said Hawkins. “Knowing this may be the first documented river otter in the Bronx in generations was an incredible moment. It shows why long-term wildlife monitoring and environmental restoration efforts matter.”
The Bronx River extends 23 miles through southeastern New York. Like many waterways that flow into and through New York City, the river became heavily polluted during the 19th and 20th century. It was often used as an open sewer and industrial waste site, which subsequently chased away much of the natural wildlife that relied on it, otters included. Since the 1970s, however, groups like the Bronx River Alliance and Bronz Zoo have been working to restore the river to its previous state.
Life returning
This otter isn’t the first former resident to make its way back to the river. Starting in 2007, a pair of beavers made their home in the area. And though these beavers have likely since passed away, camera traps last year caught footage of another beaver swimming in the river. These traps have also recently spotted other wildlife like muskrats, turtles, and many different species of birds.
This latest sighting is especially encouraging, however, because river otters are typically an indicator of a healthy freshwater system. Otters are usually near the top of the food chain, and they need plenty of aquatic prey and clean water to survive. While it’s too early to tell whether this otter and others like it are making themselves cozy in the Bronx River, there’s certainly reason to hope that things are truly changing for the better in the area, for both human residents and their wildlife neighbors.
“This otter’s return is a gift, not just to the Bronx River but to the communities that have fought for 50 years to bring this river back to life. For too long, the Bronx River was treated as a neglected afterthought, and our communities bore the burden of that neglect,” said Javier Lopez, interim executive director of the Bronx River Association. “Today, this otter reminds us that when we invest in nature, nature responds, and when communities lead, change is possible.”

title: Youth networks take lead in tackling Chhaupadi and child marriage
content:
National
Youth networks take lead in tackling Chhaupadi and child marriage
Despite resistance from families and limited support from community leaders, child club members in western Nepal are dismantling menstrual huts and helping stop underage marriages.Menuka Dhungana
It has been a year since 15-year-old Dhurba Adhikari became president of the ward-level Child Network in Panchadeval Binayak Municipality-3. Soon after taking charge, the network drew up a one-year action plan focused on social practices affecting children.
At the top of its agenda were Chhaupadi, the practice of isolating menstruating women and girls in unsafe sheds, and child marriage.
Over the past year, the network has demolished 10 Chhau sheds in the ward. Members identify the huts, talk to families and seek help from the Nepal Police and other stakeholders when necessary. Adhikari said the campaign has also helped stop five child marriages.
“We started demolishing Chhau sheds in our neighbourhood. The locals strongly resisted, but we did not back down,” Adhikari said. “We showed the same resolve in stopping child marriages and prevented five underage weddings.”
But challenging deeply rooted social practices has not been easy. Adhikari said the network receives little of the support it expects from local leaders and elected representatives, making its work more difficult.
Despite the lack of institutional backing, members are trying to lead by example in their own homes.
Ramila Shahi, 14, another network member, persuaded her family to demolish their Chhau shed.
“Going to network meetings while keeping a Chhau shed at home made me uncomfortable,” Shahi said. “My family initially refused and asked where I had learned these things. With support from my friends in the network and the police, we demolished it. I now stay inside the house during my period and encourage other families to do the same.”
Similar child-led efforts are gaining ground in other parts of Achham.
In Kamalbazar Municipality-5, Kuika, the ward-level child network has become an informal information network for preventing child marriages.
According to network member Kuber Devkota, members gather information about planned underage marriages and alert authorities. Acting on their information, ward officials and police recently tracked down and brought back 13 underage individuals who had been taken to India after getting married.
The Kuika network also promotes marriage at the legal age. The legal age of marriage in Nepal is 20. Devkota said the ward office recently honoured 25 couples who married after reaching the legal age, giving young people an incentive to wait rather than marrying as children.
The network also monitors Chhau sheds and urges families to allow women and girls to stay safely inside their homes during menstruation. Reshma Bhul, a network member, said young people regularly visit households to monitor whether families are continuing the practice.
Their persistence appears to be changing attitudes among local leaders as well.
Ratan Bhul, a ward member in Kamalbazar-5 who also serves as a traditional Dhami, or faith healer, said his own views had changed.
“I am an elected representative and a Dhami. Whatever the practices were in the past, I have now joined the campaign to ensure women remain safe inside their homes during menstruation,” he said.
By reporting planned child marriages and monitoring Chhau sheds, the young activists are challenging entrenched practices while also pushing child rights and safety higher on the local agenda.

title: Jana Van Lent, de l’enfer au paradis : “Elle a tout fait parfaitement”
content:
Jana Van Lent, de l'enfer au paradis : "Elle a tout fait parfaitement"
Le père de la médaillée de bronze du 10 000 m raconte que la coureuse de fond a bien failli ne pas se rendre à l'Euro de Birmingham : "Quelques jours plus tôt, Jana allait vraiment très mal…"
- Publié le 16-08-2026 à 15h44
Après l'arrivée du 10 000 m, Jana Van Lent a cherché du regard et trouvé son père en tribunes. Médaille de bronze autour du cou, elle s'est précipitée vers lui. "J'espérais bien pouvoir le serrer dans mes bras en premier ! J'ai pleuré. Il a pleuré. C'était un moment très spécial."
À 25 ans, l'athlète de Bornem, devancée par Nadia Battocletti et Maureen Koster, est montée sur son premier podium international après quelques places d'honneur dans les grands rendez-vous. Fini les médailles en chocolat, place à une "vraie" médaille. Et c'est sous la direction de Geert, son père et son "meilleur ami" comme elle le dit, que l'athlète de l'Excelsior y est parvenue.
"À voir son langage corporel, j'ai compris assez vite que les choses allaient bien se passer, dit le père de famille, non loin du podium. Et Jana a tout fait parfaitement ! Quand elles n'étaient plus que quatre en tête, j'ai su que c'était bon pour la médaille. Même si je suis quelqu'un de très calme, elle a fait battre mon cœur plus vite que d'habitude. Il faut prendre conscience de ce qu'elle a accompli et dans quel contexte."
Six jours plus tôt, Jana Van Lent a été victime d'une réaction allergique très grave, potentiellement fatale, dont on ne connaît pas l'origine. Elle s'était effondrée sur le sol de la cuisine.
Nous étions convaincus qu'elle ne pourrait même pas participer.
"Jana allait vraiment très mal, raconte Geert Van Lent. Nous étions convaincus qu'elle ne pourrait même pas participer à l'Euro. Finalement, nous avons quand même fait le voyage et elle a profité de chaque seconde pour se reposer. Elle n'est même pas allée au stade avant. Émotionnellement c'était les montagnes russes, mais son état de santé s'est amélioré de jour en jour. Nous étions quand même prudents quant à ses ambitions."
Le dénouement heureux de cette histoire fut un vrai soulagement pour le duo père-fille.
"Quand nous avons pleuré ensemble, elle m'a dit : 'Papa, après cette semaine de merde, nous sommes passés de l'enfer au paradis'. J'avais exactement le même sentiment, sourit Geert Van Lent. Notre lien est vraiment spécial. Il est… indescriptible. On parle de tout, je n'ai aucun secret pour elle."
8e médaillée féminine
La détentrice des records de Belgique des 3 000 m, 5 000 m et 10 000 m est la huitième médaillée belge féminine dans une épreuve individuelle à l'Euro après Kim Gevaert, Tia Hellebaut, Svetlana Bolshakova, Nafi Thiam, Noor Vidts, Delphine Nkansa et Saliyya Guisse.
"C'est la récompense de nombreuses années de travail et de l'équipe autour de moi où mon papa joue un rôle central", souligne Jana Van Lent.
Ami, coach et aussi un peu sponsor, l'homme voit sa fille prendre son envol international. Et qui sait, peut-être pourront-ils bientôt partir ensemble en stage en altitude, ce qu'ils n'ont jamais fait. "Se préparer à la maison, cela a aussi ses avantages…"

title: WNBA in Vancouver ‘surreal’ for Olympian as Tempo ends losing streak against Fire
content:
Growing up in Chatham, Ont., Bridget Carleton couldn’t imagine playing professional basketball in Canada.
This season, she’s getting the chance.
“It’s surreal,” the Portland Fire forward said before her team took on the Toronto Tempo in Vancouver on Friday. “I would never have imagined this when I was a kid growing up in Canada.”
Carleton was lucky — her mom knew about the Detroit Shock and they travelled across the border to take in some games. But the WNBA remained largely inaccessible.
“We didn’t see it on TV,” she said. “The fact that I’m 29 now, playing in Canada in a WNBA game, is just crazy. That kids have this to look up to in Canada, it’s just really cool, how much it’s evolved across America and also now Canada.”
Vancouver games show Tempo’s Canada-wide reach
An announced crowd of 12,414 watched the Tempo (11-25) claw their way back from a 13-point deficit to beat the Fire 82-79 on Friday. The result ended Toronto’s 12-game losing skid.
It was a crowd that gave the Tempo an extra boost, said centre Isabelle Harrison.
“It felt good. I just felt like we had the momentum on our side because all the fans were here,” she said. “Canada really showed up for us today.”
Portland (15-21) jumped out to an early lead, thanks in part to the nine points Carleton scored in the first six minutes of the game.
Toronto rallied, though, and levelled the score at 44-44 heading into halftime.
Fans jumped to their feet midway through the third quarter when Harrison muscled her way through traffic and put in a layup that gave Toronto a 58-53 lead.
“I’ve been told since being here, they respect hard basketball players. And they love basketball out here,” she said. “I’m just, first and foremost, into my team, playing hard for them. But making sure the crowd has something to cheer for. They showed up for us today.”
The noise inside Rogers Arena on Friday was so loud at times that Tempo head coach Sandy Brondello had trouble communicating with her teammates.
“We felt the support,” she said. “When we made big plays, it was hard for me even to talk in some of the timeouts there. I’m just happy the fans got to see us play. We are Canada’s team and they’re behind us.”
Friday’s game is part of the Tempo’s Cross Canada series, which also saw Toronto play a pair of games at Montreal’s Bell Centre in July.
The first matchup, a 108-95 loss to the Dallas Wings, drew a crowd of 20,996, setting an attendance record for a WNBA regular-season game.
Visiting different parts of the country is simply part of the Tempo’s identity, said Brondello.
“We’re trying to build more fans and show them what the Tempo is about and make these players household names,” she said. “Hopefully we can get more new fans, and not just for the Tempo, for the WNBA.”
Brondello has been part of the WNBA for 27 of its 30 seasons as either a player or a coach.
Bringing an expansion team to Canada has had its challenges, she said, but seeing the evolution of women’s basketball has been great.
“Our league has grown so much,” she said.
“We had expansions early, and it wasn’t the right time. This was the right time. I think the sponsorship and the eyes that we have on us is amazing, and the visibility. And any time that you can go to a new city, it’s an opportunity, isn’t it? So we’re a global game, but Canada is making this sport even bigger and better.”
The Tempo will stay in Vancouver for the weekend, hosting a fan festival on Saturday before taking on the Las Vegas Aces at Rogers Arena on Sunday.
The trip shows how much the league has grown in recent years, said Toronto guard Brittney Sykes.
“It’s just experiencing the type of fandom that we’re getting, the type of buy-in that we’re getting, the type of expansion that we’re getting — I wouldn’t have thought we had a team in Canada, and now we do,” she said.
“I just want us to keep putting out a really great product for these little girls and every little kid … just to believe that they can make it to the next level.”
Watching WNBA games in Canada will be huge for coming generations of basketball players across the country, Carleton said.
“Seeing women professional athletes playing so close to home, the sky’s the limit. You don’t have to have small dreams,” said the two-time Olympian.
“I think that’s the biggest thing, is what you can see, you can be. And I would have loved that as a kid. And so now I’m really honoured to be that for somebody else. To have professional women’s sports in Canada, it’s a dream come true.”

title: Emergency Housing
content:
Sarah Sherr woke to the smell of smoke at 3:30 a.m. on January 8, 2025. Pregnant, she was two weeks from her due date. She shook her husband awake, packed up their malamute and border collie, and drove away from their West Altadena home before he even had time to put on a shirt. By 7 a.m., the palm trees lining their street were ablaze. Their house was ashes two hours later.
Like tens of thousands of people in Los Angeles displaced by wildfires that week, Sherr needed somewhere to go. Scrolling on Instagram, she found a post about free Airbnb housing credits for wildfire victims. The offer came from Airbnb.org, a nonprofit that provides free emergency housing through the same platform that powers one of the world’s largest homestay companies. She filled out an application that night, and by morning she had credits in her Airbnb account. She and her husband stayed with their animals for four nights in a mountain cabin in North San Diego, then moved to a property with a pool and a garden, where they spent the first month of their newborn’s life.
“We had very limited options with our animals, and it was such a relief that we could go somewhere of our choosing,” she says. “It was such a weird time of peace and fun and stress all at once.”
Founded by Airbnb in 2020, Airbnb.org was built on a premise that the company’s platform, with its nine million listings in nearly every corner of the world, could do more than serve leisure travelers. Established as a separate 501(c)(3), the organization mobilizes that technology and infrastructure to provide free temporary housing when disaster strikes. Airbnb.org activates hosts near distressed locations, waives fees, and works through a network of local nonprofit partners to identify and refer displaced and unhoused families.
“On the surface, we’re addressing housing,” says Christoph Gorder, executive director of Airbnb.org. “Underneath it, we’re addressing a delivery mechanism. How do we get you assistance very quickly, and how do we give survivors agency.”
Repurposing the Platform
An Airbnb home provides displaced families something that makeshift shelters in school gyms and stadiums cannot. It gives them a sanctuary to grieve, to regroup, and to cook a meal. It keeps them together, and, critically, it keeps them close to the schools, jobs, and communities they depend on to rebuild their lives.
The model works through partnerships. Airbnb.org identifies trusted local nonprofits, negotiates agreements, and when a crisis hits, moves quickly. The nonprofit partner vets and refers families. Airbnb.org deposits credits directly into referred people’s Airbnb accounts. People who don’t already have an Airbnb account can create one for free, and a dedicated customer-support team helps Airbnb.org guests with the booking process. Local partners often provide help such as power and connectivity to those who have lost internet access. Families choose their own accommodations to fit their needs, and Airbnb waives all service fees.
Because Airbnb acts as Airbnb.org’s largest donor, covering all operating costs and providing additional funding for disaster responses, 100 percent of public donations go directly to housing. Airbnb.org raises the majority of its funds from the public through individual donors and Airbnb hosts. Hosts are paid as they would be for any ordinary Airbnb stay, though many choose to offer a discount for Airbnb.org guests. Any Airbnb host can participate and does not need to donate to Airbnb.org to host emergency stays, though many do choose to support the organization by donating a percentage of their earnings. Recurring host donors alone contribute roughly $2 million to the organization every year.
For nonprofit partners like All Hands and Hearts, a volunteer-run disaster-relief organization that identifies and refers displaced families to Airbnb.org, the host community is central to what makes the model work. “It’s a very meaningful way for people to feel that they can chip in beyond the obvious donation or volunteering,” says Nicolette Koeman, chief engagement officer of All Hands and Hearts.
Responding First
On the night of January 7, as fires spread rapidly across Los Angeles County, phones began ringing at 211 LA, the hub for community members and organizations looking for health, human, and social services. Many of the callers looking for help had already lost access to housing, transportation, and basic utilities.
Representatives from Airbnb.org called 211 LA Executive Director Maribel Marin, and within hours, the two organizations had signed an agreement. “We are scrappy problem-solvers,” Marin says. “We didn’t have to worry about red tape. We said, ‘Let’s do this.’”
Disaster response is Airbnb.org’s core mission, but the organization is expanding its vision.
In the first three weeks after the disaster, 211 LA handled 41,669 wildfire-related contacts. Housing emerged as the most urgent need almost immediately. Ultimately, more than 63,000 nights were donated through the partnership. In the immediate aftermath, Airbnb.org supported short-term evacuation stays for 10,452 households and coordinated longer-term 30-day placements for 321 households, totaling 8,129 nights of safe, temporary housing.
A similar response unfolded when devastating floods struck Kerr County, Texas, in the state’s Hill Country region in July 2025. There, Airbnb.org partnered with All Hands and Hearts, which identified the residents most in need and referred them to Airbnb.org. Free housing credits went to displaced residents, family members needing to stay close to search-and-rescue operations, and first-responder crews conducting relief efforts on the ground. While some just wanted a home with a backyard for the kids to run around in, others needed a pet-friendly home or accessibility features.
“Dignity and ownership are the keywords in a disaster-recovery journey,” Koeman says. “The technology and platform of Airbnb really allows us to have a very targeted, personalized, modern way of supporting people.”
Austin Dickson, CEO of the Community Foundation of the Texas Hill Country, saw the value of the model firsthand. The foundation granted Airbnb.org $1.6 million to support the Kerr County response.
“A family cannot focus on insurance claims, rebuilding plans, school enrollment, or returning to work if they don’t know where they’re sleeping next week,” Dickson says. One pregnant flood survivor, who had a toddler and a full-time job, chose the Airbnb.org option specifically because she couldn’t absorb the added burden of finding and furnishing a rental on top of everything else. “That’s survivor-centered design working as intended,” Dickson says.
The efficiency of the model also appealed to Dickson. “Their platform is already built to deliver housing at scale during crises, without requiring us to build that infrastructure ourselves.”
Expanding Beyond Disaster
Disaster response is Airbnb.org’s core mission, but the organization is expanding its vision. Its Medical Stays program provides free housing to families who must travel long distances to access specialized medical care. Gorder describes it as a Ronald McDonald House model, without the waiting list. Since spring 2026, the program has expanded to Italy, Spain, and Thailand.
In Mexico City, two nonprofit partners, Fundación Vuela and Casa de la Amistad, are already enrolling families. In May 2026, Airbnb CEO and cofounder Brian Chesky announced a commitment of more than $1 million to expand Medical Stays in Mexico over the next three years.
Childhood cancer is the leading cause of death from disease among children ages 5 to 14 in Mexico, and Mexico City receives more than 25 percent of the country’s childhood cancer patients. Families travel from every region, often with no plan for where they will sleep.
“The first thing in their minds is how to get the sick kid to the hospital,” says Diego Herrera, cofounder and CEO of Fundación Vuela. Many times they don’t even think about where they’re going to stay.”
Public hospitals offer little help. Herrera describes streets outside pediatric wards filled with parents waiting overnight for visiting hours, sleeping on sidewalks, unable to bathe or rest. Existing shelters typically allow only one parent and one patient, leaving single parents with the hard decision to leave their other children behind. The consequences can be deadly. In Mexico, Herrera says, treatment for an estimated 20 percent of childhood cancer patients is abandoned when the logistical and financial burden of staying in the city becomes too great.
In the first six months of operating Medical Stays in Mexico City, Airbnb.org and its partners provided nearly 300 nights of free housing to more than 50 families. For many, the experience required learning new technology. Guided by Vuela staff, some families were using a smartphone app for the first time, navigating an email account and digital transactions entirely foreign to them.
Leo was among the first patients in the program. When the shuttle taking him and his mother got stuck in traffic, their Airbnb host, Erick, drove his own car to pick them up, showed them the neighborhood, and pointed out restaurants. Days later, Leo told Herrera that even though his mother wasn’t allowed to stay overnight at the hospital, he could sleep peacefully knowing she was safe and resting nearby.
Another patient, Romina, suffered from nausea after chemotherapy and struggled to eat the hospital food. Back at her Airbnb, her mother cooked a meal and was able to encourage her daughter to eat.
“Cancer is hard enough,” Herrera says. “Nothing should make it worse.”
Becoming Proactive
In its six years of existence, Airbnb.org has only found ever-greater need for its services. In 2023, Airbnb.org responded to eight disasters. In 2024, that number grew to 18. In 2025, it jumped to 78, including the LA wildfires, Hurricane Melissa in the Caribbean, and the Central Texas floods. Responses in 2026 already include Winter Storm Fern in Nashville, Tropical Storm Nils in France, and the earthquakes in Venezuela. The Medical Stays program is growing across multiple continents.
Airbnb.org can deploy housing credits wherever its platform reaches. But it is limited by its ability to partner with trusted local nonprofits already embedded in communities, preferably before disaster strikes. First-time responses with first-time partners can be slower and messier. Take the complexity faced by 211 LA managing 51,000 contacts in the first days of the fires. Organizers grappled with data duplication, scattered families, and the challenge of reaching people who feared a callback from an unknown number was a scam.
“We wouldn’t have struggled as much if we had some of these partnerships in place before the fire started,” Marin says.
Even when agreements are in place, the sheer volume of need can overwhelm operations on all sides. In Los Angeles, Gorder admits that as demand exploded in the first days of the fires, Airbnb.org’s own phone banks were crushed. Processing tens of thousands of families simultaneously, verifying eligibility, depositing credits, and troubleshooting placements tested the organization’s infrastructure.
Dickson echoes the lesson from Texas. “Relationships built after a disaster are always going to be slower and less effective than relationships built before one. When the disaster happened, we weren’t introducing ourselves. We were activating relationships that already existed.”
Airbnb.org has begun building more associations in advance. It has formalized disaster-preparedness partnerships with government agencies and community organizations in Los Angeles, Japan, and Mexico City, alongside standing agreements with Catholic Charities across its 168 US chapters and with 211 networks nationwide. Most recently, Airbnb.org signed an agreement with the Secretariat for Integrated Risk Management and Civil Protection, Mexico City’s disaster response agency, to provide free stays for first responders and volunteer groups who deploy to communities impacted by disasters throughout the country.
“The need continues to rise, and we see it happening with climate change all around us,” Koeman says. “There is no way that authorities can cope with this level of need on such a big scale. So it is going to require all of us, civil society and private entities, to come together to really support the need that exists.”
As Airbnb.org has expanded, Gorder says, the organization has shifted from reactive to proactive. His team has developed country-level plans and pre-signed agreements designed to speed up the time between crisis and housing.
“The question is not whether we will have more disasters,” he says. “The question is, how quickly can we help, and how much agency can we give people in the worst moments of their lives?”

title: CET: Final seat allotment result announced
content:
The Karnataka Examinations Authority (KEA) on Monday announced the final results of the second round of seat allotment for admission to UG CET courses, including engineering.
The admission process for CET courses will be open from August 25 to August 28. Candidates allotted seats can pay the prescribed fee and report to the respective college during this period, said KEA Executive Director H. Prasanna.
Candidates allotted seats in Engineering, Architecture, Yoga and Naturopathy, Agricultural Sciences, Veterinary Science, B.Sc. Nursing, B.Pharm, Pharm-D, BPT, BPO and Allied Health Sciences can choose Choice 1, pay the fee and take admission if they are satisfied with the allotted seat. Those who do not want the allotted seat can select Choice 4 and exit the counselling process.
Candidates who select Choice 1, join the CET course and still hope to get a better seat can participate in the third round of seat allotment by logging in.
However, candidates who do not select Choice 1 but wish to participate in the third round must first cancel the seat allotted to them in the second round by paying a ₹5,000 penalty. They can then log in, pay the registration fee afresh and participate in the third round, Mr. Prasanna said.
